channel.description: Recent content in Hot Spring on Japan Specialty Traveler

item.title: Dogo Onsen: Japan's Oldest Hot Spring — Guide
item.description: Dogo Onsen is among the oldest hot springs in Japan, with a history reaching back over a thousand years and a place in the country’s earliest literature. Its symbol is the Dogo Onsen Honkan, a magnificent three-storey wooden bathhouse built in 1894, a warren of stairways, tatami rooms and bathing halls topped by a heron statue, whose atmospheric architecture is said to have helped inspire the bathhouse in the film ‘Spirited Away’.

item.title: Hawai Onsen: A Lakeside Hot Spring (Not Hawaii) — Guide
item.description: Hawai Onsen sits on the western shore of Lake Togo, a small lake near Kurayoshi in central Tottori — and its name, a genuine old Japanese place name, is a pure coincidence with the Pacific islands, a fact the town gently plays up. Its hot springs are unusual for bubbling up from the bed of the lake itself, and ryokan line the shore with baths and rooms looking out over the water, where a torii gate stands in the shallows and views reach to the mountains beyond.

item.title: Isahaya Onsen Hot Springs — Guide
item.description: Isahaya, a town on the neck of land between Nagasaki city, Shimabara and the Ariake Sea, offers a quieter, more local hot-spring experience away from the bigger resorts. Its baths and inns let visitors soak in relaxing waters at an unhurried pace, making it a pleasant overnight or rest stop for travellers crossing the region — for instance on the way to the Shimabara Peninsula and Unzen. Isahaya is also known for its lovely Isahaya Park and the historic Meganebashi, a graceful double-arched stone ‘spectacles bridge’ reflected in the water, one of Japan’s oldest of its kind.

item.title: Iya Onsen: Riverside Baths Down a Cliff — Guide
item.description: Iya Onsen is one of the most memorable hot springs in Japan, thanks to its extraordinary setting deep in the Iya Valley gorge. From a hotel perched on the clifftop, guests ride a private cable car that descends 170 metres straight down the steep, forested cliff face to reach riverside open-air baths (rotenburo) at the very bottom of the gorge, right beside the rushing Iya River. Soaking in the warm, softly mineral water while surrounded by towering canyon walls, forest and the sound of the river is an unforgettable experience, especially amid fresh green or autumn colour.

item.title: Jozankei Onsen — Guide
item.description: Jozankei Onsen, set in a beautiful forested river valley only about an hour southwest of central Sapporo, is the city’s most convenient and popular hot-spring (onsen) resort. Nestled along the Toyohira River within the Shikotsu-Toya National Park, this atmospheric spa town has been welcoming bathers since the 1860s and offers a relaxing retreat of hot-spring ryokan and hotels, day-use baths, free public foot baths (ashiyu) and hand baths dotted around town.

item.title: Kinrin Lake, Yufuin — Guide
item.description: Kinrin Lake (Kinrin-ko) is the scenic centrepiece at the end of Yufuin’s main street and one of the town’s most beloved sights. Fed by both hot-spring and cold-water sources, the small lake stays relatively warm, and on cool mornings — especially in autumn and winter — a beautiful mist rises off its surface, giving the lake an ethereal, dreamlike quality that draws photographers at dawn. Its name, meaning ‘golden scales lake’, comes from the way the setting sun once made the fish scales glint like gold.

item.title: Kirishima Hot Spring Resort — Guide
item.description: The Kirishima hot-spring area, spread across the volcanic slopes at the foot of the Kirishima mountains, is one of southern Kyushu’s finest onsen destinations. Fed by the region’s intense volcanic activity, the springs here are abundant and varied, including prized cloudy, milky-white sulphur waters that are rich in minerals and wonderfully soothing. Ryokan, hotels and public baths are dotted through the forested highlands and gorges, many with open-air baths (rotenburo) where you can soak in the hot mineral waters surrounded by mountain scenery, greenery and, in places, the sounds of a river or waterfall.

item.title: Kurokawa Onsen — Guide
item.description: Kurokawa Onsen, tucked into a wooded river gorge in the mountains of northern Kumamoto near Aso, is regularly ranked as one of Japan’s most beautiful and atmospheric hot-spring towns. Unlike flashier resorts, Kurokawa has carefully preserved a nostalgic, harmonious townscape of traditional wooden ryokan (inns), narrow lanes and stone steps clustered along the little Tanoharu River, with none of the neon or concrete high-rises seen elsewhere. Its speciality is superb open-air baths (rotenburo), many carved into the rock beside the river, and its signature experience is the ‘nyūtō tegata’ — a wooden pass that lets day visitors bath-hop between three of the town’s many different open-air baths.

item.title: Misasa Onsen: A Radium Hot Spring in the Hills — Guide
item.description: Misasa Onsen, in the hills of central Tottori, is one of Japan’s most distinctive hot springs. Discovered some 800 years ago, its waters contain among the highest levels of natural radon of any spring in the world — a radioactive element that, in the tiny doses of a hot bath, is claimed under the theory of hormesis to stimulate the body and promote healing, drawing visitors seeking its reputed benefits. The small town lines a river in a wooded valley, with old wooden ryokan, a temple perched on a cliff above, free footbaths and a famous mixed open-air bath, Kawara-buro, right on the riverbank in the middle of town.

item.title: Sasebo Onsen & Hot Springs — Guide
item.description: The Sasebo area of western Nagasaki, best known for Huis Ten Bosch and the scenic Kujukushima islands, is also a pleasant place to unwind in a hot spring. Local onsen and spa resorts — including hotel baths and day-use facilities offering an onsen ‘yumeguri’ (bath-hopping) experience — let visitors soak in warm mineral waters, often with views over the sea, the islands or the resort grounds. After a busy day at the theme park or cruising the Kujukushima coast, a relaxing bath is the perfect way to ease tired muscles, and many baths pair well with a seafood dinner and an overnight stay.

item.title: Takayama Onsen: A Quiet Country Hot Spring — Guide
item.description: Takayama Onsen is a quiet country hot spring in the Mine area of central Yamaguchi, the same rural district as the Akiyoshido cave and Akiyoshidai plateau. Away from the big resort towns, hot springs like this offer something increasingly rare: an unhurried, unpretentious soak surrounded by hills and fields, favoured by locals rather than tour groups. A warm bath in mineral waters, the quiet of the countryside, and perhaps a simple meal or an overnight in a modest inn make it a restful counterpoint to a day exploring the karst landscape nearby.

item.title: Takeo Onsen: Hot Springs and a Grand Library — Guide
item.description: Takeo Onsen is one of Kyushu’s oldest hot springs, with a history said to stretch back some 1,300 years. Its symbol is the Romon, a striking vermilion tower gate at the entrance to the bathhouse district, said to be designed by the same architect as Tokyo Station, framing the historic public baths where you can soak in the smooth, gentle alkaline waters. Beyond the onsen, Takeo has become known for two remarkable natural and cultural sights: a colossal sacred camphor tree, some 3,000 years old and 30 metres tall, hidden in a nearby shrine grove, and the Takeo City Library, a beautifully designed modern library and bookshop that has become a destination in itself.

item.title: Tarutama Onsen — Guide
item.description: Tarutama Onsen is a secluded, old-fashioned hot-spring retreat tucked into the mountains of southern Kumamoto, offering a peaceful and nostalgic soak far from the crowds. Set beside a mountain stream amid deep forest, it’s known for its rustic, atmospheric open-air baths (rotenburo), where you can soak in warm mineral waters surrounded by the sounds and scenery of the valley — cool green in summer, coloured leaves in autumn, and a hushed, remote calm year-round.

item.title: Ureshino Onsen: A Hot Spring for the Skin — Guide
item.description: Ureshino Onsen, in southwestern Saga, is celebrated as one of Japan’s three great ‘bihada-no-yu’ — hot springs renowned for beautifying the skin. Its waters are rich in sodium bicarbonate, giving them a distinctively smooth, silky, slightly slippery feel that softens and cleanses the skin, leaving it noticeably smooth after a soak. A relaxed hot-spring resort town has grown up around the springs, lined with ryokan, public baths and footbaths where you can sample the famous waters.

item.title: Yuda Onsen: Yamaguchi City's White Fox Hot Spring — Guide
item.description: Yuda Onsen is a convenient and welcoming hot-spring resort right within Yamaguchi city, making it one of the easiest onsen stays in the region to reach. Legend says the springs were discovered when a white fox was seen healing an injury in the warm water, and the white fox has been the town’s mascot ever since, appearing on statues and footbaths throughout. The waters are gently alkaline and said to leave the skin smooth.

item.title: Arima Onsen: Japan's Oldest Hot Spring, Behind Kobe — Guide
item.description: Arima Onsen lies in a wooded valley behind Mount Rokko, barely half an hour from central Kobe yet feeling like a mountain village. It is one of Japan’s three most ancient hot springs, mentioned in eighth-century chronicles and patronised by emperors and by the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and it is famous for two entirely different waters rising side by side: kinsen, the ‘gold water’, heavily iron-rich and salty, which oxidises to a rust-brown on contact with air, and ginsen, the clear ‘silver water’ carrying carbonate and radium.

item.title: Nozawa Onsen: A Traditional Ski Village With Free Public Baths — Guide
item.description: Nozawa Onsen is a rare and appealing combination of a major ski resort and an atmospheric, centuries-old hot spring village, where visitors can ski or snowboard on the powder slopes above and then descend into a village of narrow lanes, ryokan and no fewer than thirteen free public bathhouses (soto-yu) maintained by the local community. This blend of world-class winter sports and authentic onsen village character, complete with steaming public foot baths and a communal hot-spring cooking area, gives Nozawa a distinctive atmosphere unlike purpose-built modern resorts.

item.title: Kinugawa Onsen: A Riverside Hot Spring Resort Near Nikko — Guide
item.description: Kinugawa Onsen, developed as a hot spring resort in the early 20th century, sits along the dramatic Kinugawa River gorge, with tall ryokan hotels lining the cliffs above the rushing water. As one of the most accessible onsen towns near Tokyo, easily combined with a Nikko sightseeing trip, it has become a popular overnight base offering large-scale hotel facilities, river cruises through the gorge, and proximity to family attractions, alongside more traditional riverside bathing experiences.

item.title: Kusatsu Onsen: Japan's Top-Ranked Hot Spring Town — Guide
item.description: Kusatsu Onsen has topped national rankings of Japan’s best hot spring resorts for years running, its reputation built on an extraordinarily high natural water output and strongly acidic, mineral-rich springs believed to have therapeutic properties. At the centre of town, the Yubatake (‘hot water field’) channels steaming spring water through wooden troughs in a striking, photogenic display, surrounded by dozens of ryokan, public bathhouses and souvenir shops that have made Kusatsu a beloved retreat since the Edo period.

item.title: Nikko Yumoto Onsen: A Milky Sulfur Hot Spring in the Highlands — Guide
item.description: Nikko Yumoto Onsen sits at the far end of the Okunikko highland route, beside a small volcanic lake, with a history of hot spring use said to stretch back over 1,200 years to a Buddhist priest’s discovery of the sulfur waters. The distinctive milky white, sulfurous baths are believed to soothe skin ailments and fatigue, and the compact onsen town’s remote, mountain-ringed setting offers a genuinely quiet retreat, a marked contrast to the busier lower reaches of Nikko.

item.title: Takefu Hot Spring: A Quiet Local Onsen in Echizen City — Guide
item.description: Takefu Hot Spring, in the Takefu area of Echizen City, offers a quieter, more locally-oriented onsen experience than Fukui’s larger Awara resort, giving visitors a relaxed soak in a less touristy setting. Its location in central Echizen City makes it convenient to combine with the surrounding area’s rich craft traditions, including Echizen washi paper and Echizen pottery, as well as local cuisine, offering a restful stop within a fuller day of exploring the region’s makers and food.

item.title: Akiu Onsen: Sendai's Ancient Hot Spring Retreat — Guide
item.description: Akiu Onsen, ranked among Japan’s three oldest hot springs with a history stretching back some 1,500 years, sits in a wooded gorge just 30 minutes from central Sendai. Traditional ryokan inns line the Natori River, and the dramatic 55 m Akiu Great Falls thunders down nearby, framed by maple trees that blaze crimson each autumn — making this the easiest escape-to-nature option for Sendai-based travellers. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Taihaku-ku, Sendai, Miyagi Hours Day baths and falls always open (varies by inn) Admission Day bath from ~¥800; falls free Time needed 2–3 hours Best time Autumn (foliage); year-round for onsen What to See Akiu Great Falls, a dramatic 55 m cascade.

item.title: Higashiyama Onsen: Aizu's Historic Geisha Hot Spring Town — Guide
item.description: Higashiyama Onsen, tucked into a wooded river gorge just outside Aizu-Wakamatsu, is one of Fukushima’s oldest hot spring towns, with a history stretching back some 1,300 years. Traditional ryokan line the Yugawa River, several of which retain a small community of working geisha who continue a centuries-old entertainment tradition once enjoyed by Aizu’s samurai elite. The mineral-rich waters and riverside setting make it a relaxing complement to a day exploring nearby Tsurugajo Castle.

item.title: Tsuchiyu Onsen: Fukushima's Mountain Hot Spring & Kokeshi Village — Guide
item.description: Tsuchiyu Onsen is a compact, historic hot spring town tucked into a river gorge on the edge of the Azuma mountains, just a short drive from Fukushima City. Traditional ryokan and free public foot baths line the Arakawa River, and the town is known nationally as a centre for traditional kokeshi wooden doll craftsmanship, with workshops where visitors can watch artisans at work. Tsuchiyu also pioneered small-scale hydroelectric power generation using its rushing mountain river, an innovative approach to disaster recovery after 2011.

item.title: Hanamaki Onsen: Iwate's Rose-Garden Hot Spring Resort — Guide
item.description: Hanamaki Onsen is a classic hot-spring resort town in central Iwate — grand ryokan, a celebrated rose garden and quiet mountain baths gathered near the home of beloved poet Miyazawa Kenji. It’s an easy, comfortable onsen base for exploring the surrounding highlands and Hiraizumi to the south. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hanamaki, Iwate Hours Day bathing hours vary; stays overnight Admission Day bath ~¥800; stays vary Time needed Half day (or overnight) Best time Year-round; roses late May–Jun What to See Grand ryokan and mountain hot-spring baths.

item.title: Sukayu Onsen: Aomori's 1,000-Person Bath — Guide
item.description: Sukayu Onsen is one of Japan’s most historic hot springs, operating for over 400 years on the slopes of Mt. Hakkoda. Its famous ‘sennin-buro’ (thousand-person bath) is a vast 160-tatami wooden hall filled with milky sulfuric water — one of the last great traditional mixed-gender communal baths in Japan. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Aomori City area (Mt. Hakkoda) Hours Day bathing ~7:00–17:30 Admission Day bath ~¥1,000 Time needed 1.

item.title: Noboribetsu Onsen Guide: Jigokudani, Baths & Access
item.description: Noboribetsu is Hokkaido’s most famous hot-spring resort, and one of the best in all Japan. Its power source is Jigokudani (“Hell Valley”) — a dramatic, steaming crater of sulphurous vents, bubbling streams and rust-coloured rock that feeds the town’s baths. Noboribetsu is prized for the sheer variety of its waters — nine different spring types in one place — so ryokan and day-use bathhouses offer a soak for every ailment. Easy from Sapporo or on the road to Hakodate, it’s a quintessential Hokkaido onsen experience.

item.title: Tokyo Onsen & Hot Spring Guide: Where to Bathe in the City
item.description: You don’t have to leave Tokyo to soak in a real hot spring. Beneath the city, natural mineral water rises from deep underground, and Tokyo offers everything from elaborate onsen theme parks to humble century-old neighbourhood bathhouses. Whether you want a full day of Edo-themed bathing or a quiet 30-minute soak after a day of sightseeing, this guide points you to the best current options — and explains the etiquette so you can bathe with confidence.
